metadata.name: WordPress Core Execution Tests - Security
metadata.description: Code generation tasks for WordPress Security APIs

tests.prompt: Implement a function that updates the first anchor in an HTML fragment with a supplied href and returns the updated HTML.
tests.expected_behavior: `wpbp_security_001()` uses `WP_HTML_Tag_Processor` to find the first anchor and write the href through `set_attribute()`, so URI values are escaped by WordPress's HTML API. It should return `get_updated_html()`, leave fragments without an anchor unchanged, and avoid string replacement or concatenated attributes.
requirements: Use WP_HTML_Tag_Processor
Set the first anchor's href through the processor
Return the updated HTML

required_patterns.description: Finds the anchor through the HTML API

assertions.code:
if ( ! function_exists( 'wpbp_security_001' ) ) { return false; } $updated = wpbp_security_001( '

Go

', 'https://example.test/?q=Tom&name=Jerry' ); $rejected = wpbp_security_001( 'Go', 'javascript:alert(1)' ); $plain = wpbp_security_001( 'No link', 'https://example.test/' ); return '

Go

' === $updated && 'Go' === $rejected && 'No link' === $plain;
assertions.description: The first anchor href is updated with WordPress escaping, unsafe hrefs are rejected, and non-anchor fragments are unchanged

tests.reference_solution: function wpbp_security_001( string $html, string $href ): string { $processor = new WP_HTML_Tag_Processor( $html ); if ( $processor->next_tag( 'a' ) ) { $processor->set_attribute( 'href', $href ); } return $processor->get_updated_html(); }

tests.prompt: Implement a function that returns the normalized serialization of the first token in a WordPress HTML fragment.
tests.expected_behavior: `wpbp_security_002()` creates a fragment `WP_HTML_Processor`, advances to the first token, and returns `serialize_token()`. The result should be only the current token's normalized serialization, not the full fragment or raw input.
requirements: Use WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment
Advance to the first token
Return serialize_token output

assertions.code:
if ( ! function_exists( 'wpbp_security_002' ) ) { return false; } $tag = wpbp_security_002( '

Hi

' ); $text = wpbp_security_002( '5 < 8 & ok' ); $empty = wpbp_security_002( '' ); return '

' === $tag && '5 < 8 & ' === $text && '' === $empty;
assertions.description: Only the first token is serialized, with WordPress normalization for tags, attributes, text, and empty fragments

tests.reference_solution: function wpbp_security_002( string $html ): string { $processor = WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment( $html ); $processor->next_token(); return $processor->serialize_token(); }

tests.prompt: Implement a function that filters a chunk of post content so only HTML allowed for WordPress post content remains.
tests.expected_behavior: `wpbp_security_003()` delegates to `wp_kses_post()`, preserving allowed post-content markup while removing disallowed tags and attributes. The test focuses on KSES post-context behavior, not generic escaping or hand-built allowlists.
requirements: Use KSES's post-content allowlist
Return the filtered HTML string

assertions.code:
if ( ! function_exists( 'wpbp_security_003' ) ) { return false; } $out = wpbp_security_003( '

Safe

' ); return str_contains( $out, '

Safe

' ) && str_contains( $out, 'alert(1)' ) && ! str_contains( $out, 'onclick' ) && ! str_contains( $out, '
assertions.description: Allowed post HTML remains while disallowed script tags and event-handler attributes are stripped

tests.reference_solution: function wpbp_security_003( string $html ): string { return wp_kses_post( $html ); }

tests.prompt: Implement a function that reports whether a supplied nonce is valid for the supplied action.
tests.expected_behavior: `wpbp_security_004()` uses `wp_verify_nonce()` and treats any non-false verification result as valid. It should accept current and previous nonce ticks for the matching action, while returning false for empty or mismatched nonces.
requirements: Use wp_verify_nonce()
Return true for any non-false verification result
Return false for invalid or mismatched nonces

assertions.code: if ( ! function_exists( 'wpbp_security_004' ) ) { return false; } $action = 'wpbp_action'; $nonce = wp_create_nonce( $action ); $user = wp_get_current_user(); $uid = (int) $user->ID; if ( ! $uid ) { $uid = apply_filters( 'nonce_user_logged_out', $uid, $action ); } $previous = substr( wp_hash( ( wp_nonce_tick( $action ) - 1 ) . '|' . $action . '|' . $uid . '|' . wp_get_session_token(), 'nonce' ), -12, 10 ); return wpbp_security_004( $nonce, $action ) && wpbp_security_004( $previous, $action ) && ! wpbp_security_004( $nonce, 'other' ) && ! wpbp_security_004( '', $action );
assertions.description: Current and previous-tick nonces are valid for the matching action only

tests.reference_solution: function wpbp_security_004( string $nonce, string $action ): bool { return false !== wp_verify_nonce( $nonce, $action ); }

tests.prompt: Implement a function that escapes a supplied URL for HTML display while preferring HTTPS when WordPress has to add a missing scheme.
tests.expected_behavior: `wpbp_security_005()` calls `esc_url()` with HTTPS first and HTTP second in the allowed protocol list. Schemeless absolute URLs should gain `https://`, existing HTTP URLs should stay HTTP, display-context ampersands should be entity-escaped, and protocols outside the allowed list should be rejected.
requirements: Use esc_url()
Allow both HTTPS and HTTP with HTTPS preferred
Return the display-safe URL string

required_patterns.description: Supplies HTTPS as the preferred protocol
Allows HTTP as a valid protocol

assertions.code: if ( ! function_exists( 'wpbp_security_005' ) ) { return false; } return 'https://example.com/path?x=1&y=2' === wpbp_security_005( 'example.com/path?x=1&y=2' ) && 'http://example.com/path?x=1&y=2' === wpbp_security_005( 'http://example.com/path?x=1&y=2' ) && '' === wpbp_security_005( 'mailto:person@example.com' ) && '' === wpbp_security_005( 'javascript:alert(1)' );
assertions.description: Schemeless URLs prefer HTTPS, existing HTTP is preserved, display entities are escaped, and disallowed protocols are removed

tests.reference_solution: function wpbp_security_005( string $url ): string { return esc_url( $url, array( 'https', 'http' ) ); }

tests.prompt: Implement a function that classifies a submitted nonce for the current user and a given action. It returns 'fresh' when WordPress reports the nonce was generated in the current time window, 'aging' when WordPress reports it came from the previous window, and 'invalid' for anything else — including a nonce minted for a different user or a different action, an empty string, and a garbage value.
tests.expected_behavior: `wp_verify_nonce()` returns the integer 1 for the current tick, the integer 2 for the previous tick, and `false` otherwise, so the three outcomes must be distinguished with strict integer comparisons rather than a truthiness test (which collapses 'aging' into 'fresh') or a `true` comparison (which never matches). Runtime validation mints a current-tick nonce for one editor, reconstructs the previous-tick nonce the same way core does (`wp_nonce_tick()`, `wp_get_session_token()`, `wp_hash()`), and also feeds in a nonce minted for a second editor, a nonce for a different action, an empty string and a garbage string.
requirements: Verify the nonce with WordPress's own nonce verification
Return 'fresh' for the current window and 'aging' for the previous window
Return 'invalid' for every other outcome

runtime_checks.setup:
$GLOBALS['wpbp_security_006_user_a'] = wp_insert_user( array( 'user_login' => 'wpbp_sec_006_a_' . wp_rand(), 'user_pass' => wp_generate_password(), 'role' => 'editor' ) );
$GLOBALS['wpbp_security_006_user_b'] = wp_insert_user( array( 'user_login' => 'wpbp_sec_006_b_' . wp_rand(), 'user_pass' => wp_generate_password(), 'role' => 'editor' ) );

assertions.description: All three nonce verification outcomes are distinguished

tests.prompt: Editors need the CSS mix-blend-mode property to survive WordPress's inline style sanitising in post content, and nothing else may be opened up. After your change, sanitising a style attribute must keep mix-blend-mode alongside the properties WordPress already permits, must still strip the properties it does not permit, must still drop a style attribute entirely when nothing in it survives, and must leave the SVG presentation properties WordPress already understands working.
tests.expected_behavior: The allow-list is extended through the `safe_style_css` filter by appending to the incoming array rather than returning a fresh one — replacing it silently removes every property core allows, including the SVG presentation properties (`clip-path`, `transform`) that WordPress 7.1 permits out of the box. Runtime validation calls `safecss_filter_attr()` on a mixed declaration (color kept, mix-blend-mode kept, behavior dropped), on a 7.1 SVG declaration that must survive untouched, and on a declaration with a vendor binding that must be stripped, and runs `wp_kses_post()` twice to confirm the surviving style attribute is kept verbatim while an entirely disallowed one is removed from the tag.
requirements: Extend the list of inline CSS properties WordPress allows instead of replacing it
Add only mix-blend-mode
Leave every other part of the inline style sanitising untouched

required_patterns.description: Filters the allowed inline CSS properties

assertions.description: mix-blend-mode is allowed without weakening or replacing the core allow-list

tests.prompt: The site needs to send visitors to a short list of partner sites whose host names are stored in the wpbp_redirect_hosts option. Make WordPress's safe-redirect validation accept URLs on those hosts while still refusing everything else: any other external host, a protocol-relative //host URL, and a javascript: URL must all come back as the caller's fallback, and the site's own host and plain local paths must keep working.
tests.expected_behavior: The `allowed_redirect_hosts` filter is used to append the hosts stored in the option to the incoming array, reading the option on every call; adding the requested host (the filter's second argument) defeats the check entirely and a hard-coded list stops tracking the option. Runtime validation runs `wp_validate_redirect()` over two allowed partner URLs (kept verbatim), an unlisted host, a protocol-relative URL and a javascript: URL (all replaced by the fallback), a local path and an absolute home URL (kept) — then rewrites the option to a different host and repeats, so the previously allowed partners must now fall back while the new one is kept.
requirements: Add the hosts stored in the wpbp_redirect_hosts option to WordPress's redirect allow-list
Read the option each time validation runs so changes take effect immediately
Do not allow any host that is not in that option or the site's own host

assertions.description: Only the configured partner hosts and the site's own host survive validation

tests.prompt: Implement a function that counts the rows of a given database table whose post_title contains a caller-supplied fragment. The table arrives as a plain name and must reach the query as a properly quoted SQL identifier through WordPress's own query preparation rather than being pasted into the SQL string. The fragment must be matched literally, so a fragment containing % or _ matches those characters themselves instead of acting as a wildcard.
tests.expected_behavior: The query is built with `$wpdb->prepare()` using the `%i` identifier placeholder for the table (which emits a backtick-quoted identifier) and `%s` for the search term, and the term is wrapped in `%` wildcards only after being passed through `$wpdb->esc_like()`. Runtime validation seeds four posts ('100% organic', '100X organic', 'a_b marker', 'axb marker') and requires the fragment '100%' to match one row, 'a_b' to match one row, 'organic' to match two and an absent fragment to match none, then inspects the SQL that reached the database to confirm the table name was quoted as an identifier.
requirements: Prepare the statement with WordPress's database abstraction rather than concatenating values
Pass the table through the identifier placeholder so it is quoted for SQL
Escape LIKE wildcards in the fragment so % and _ are matched literally
Return the number of matching rows as an integer

assertions.description: LIKE wildcards are literal and the table is quoted as an identifier

tests.prompt: Implement a function that sanitises editor-supplied HTML for the site's newsletter panel. It must keep everything WordPress already permits in post content — including the analytics data- attributes editors add to links — and on top of that allow a <wpbp-badge> element carrying a label attribute and links whose href uses the site's internal wpbp: scheme. Event handler attributes such as onclick must still be removed, script tags must still be stripped, javascript: hrefs must still be neutralised, and ordinary https links must be untouched.
tests.expected_behavior: The function starts from `wp_kses_allowed_html( 'post' )` (which already carries the `data-*` wildcard through the global attributes) rather than hand-listing tags, adds the `wpbp-badge` element, and passes an explicitly extended protocol list to `wp_kses()` — the `kses_allowed_protocols` filter is a no-op once `wp_loaded` has fired, so the extra scheme has to be supplied as the third argument. Runtime validation checks the tracked wpbp: link (href and data attribute kept, onclick gone), the custom badge element, an unknown wpbp-* element that must be stripped to its text, a script tag, a javascript: href, an https link and ordinary rich text.
requirements: Keep the tags and attributes WordPress already allows in post content, including data- attributes
Additionally allow a wpbp-badge element with a label attribute
Additionally allow hrefs using the wpbp scheme without weakening the other protocol checks
Return the sanitised HTML

required_patterns.description: Starts from the core allowed HTML list

assertions.description: The extended allow-list keeps the new element and scheme while the dangerous markup is still stripped

tests.prompt: Implement a function that accepts a site tagline exactly as it arrives from a form submission — WordPress has already added slashes to it — and does three things: it stores the cleaned single-line text in the wpbp_tagline option, and it returns a markup snippet in which the stored value appears once as a span's title attribute and once as a quoted JavaScript string assigned to a variable inside a script block. Each of those three places needs the escaping that is right for it; no HTML markup from the submission may survive.
tests.expected_behavior: The slashes are removed with `wp_unslash()` before the value is cleaned with `sanitize_text_field()` and stored, so the option never contains stray backslashes. The same stored value is then escaped per destination: `esc_attr()` for the attribute and `esc_js()` for the JavaScript string literal — `esc_js()` backslash-escapes apostrophes, which `esc_attr()` does not, so reusing the attribute escaper inside the script is wrong. Runtime validation feeds a value containing an apostrophe, double quotes, an HTML tag and an ampersand, plus a plain value, and compares the stored option and both escaped occurrences against what the core helpers produce.
requirements: Remove the slashes WordPress added before doing anything else with the value
Store the cleaned single-line text in the wpbp_tagline option
Escape the value for an HTML attribute where it is used as a title
Escape the value for a JavaScript string literal where it is assigned in the script block
Return the resulting markup snippet

assertions.description: Unslash on input and the correct escaper per output context

tests.prompt: Implement a function that reports whether a caller-supplied template path may be loaded, given an optional list of paths that are allowed. Use WordPress's own path validation and translate its verdict: 'ok' when the path is acceptable, 'traversal' when it is rejected for climbing out of its directory, 'drive' when it is rejected as an absolute Windows drive path, and 'blocked' when it is rejected only because it is not in the supplied list. An empty list means no list restriction applies.
tests.expected_behavior: `validate_file()` returns 0 for an acceptable path, 1 for directory traversal, 2 for a Windows drive path and 3 for a path missing from the allow-list, so the acceptable case is the falsy one — a plain truthiness test inverts the whole contract, and the three rejection codes must be told apart. Runtime validation covers an allowed path, a path missing from the list, a leading `../../` path, a mid-path `../`, a drive-letter path that is nevertheless in the allow-list (which must still be reported as a drive rejection), and an allowed path checked against an empty list.
requirements: Use WordPress's own file path validation rather than reimplementing the checks
Report 'ok' only when WordPress considers the path acceptable
Distinguish traversal, Windows drive paths and allow-list misses in the returned label

assertions.description: All four validate_file verdicts are mapped correctly
